questions.prompt: In −Σ y log ŷ for next-token prediction, y is 1 for the real next token and 0 for every other token. What does the sum reduce to?

options.text: Minus the log of the probability the model gave to the real next token.
options.explanation: Right. Every term with y = 0 drops out, so only −1 × log ŷ for the real token is left.

options.text: Minus the sum of the logs of every token's probability.
options.explanation: That would be true only if y were 1 for every token. y is 0 for the wrong tokens, so their terms become 0.

options.text: Always 0, because most y values are 0.

questions.prompt: Model A has a mean cross-entropy of 0.5 on a text. Model B has 1.0 on the same text. Using the OpenAI cookbook's perplexity rule, which is more confident?

options.text: Model B, because a bigger number means a stronger model.
options.explanation: For loss and perplexity, lower is better. The OpenAI cookbook says a higher perplexity indicates a more uncertain result.

options.text: Model A: its perplexity is e^0.5 ≈ 1.65, lower than B's e^1 ≈ 2.72.
options.explanation: Right. Perplexity is e to the minus mean logprob, which is the mean cross-entropy. Lower perplexity means a more confident result.

options.text: Neither: perplexity needs logprobs, so it can't be computed from cross-entropy.
options.explanation: The mean cross-entropy is the negative of the average logprob. Raise e to it and you have the perplexity.

options.text: They are the same, because both losses are under 2.
options.explanation: There is no cut-off at 2. 0.5 and 1.0 are different losses, and their perplexities (1.65 and 2.72) are different too.
